articles.title: Stop detecting AI content. Start signing it at the source
articles.excerpt: Every few months someone ships a new way to detect AI-generated text or images, and every few months someone else shows how to strip it. Paraphrase the text, crop or re-encode the image, and the hidde…
articles.body: Every few months someone ships a new way to detect AI-generated text or images, and every few months someone else shows how to strip it. Paraphrase the text, crop or re-encode the image, and the hidden signal gets weaker or disappears. Detection is a cat and mouse game, and the mouse only needs to win once. There is a calmer way to think about this. Instead of asking "can I prove this was made by AI?", ask "can I prove where this came from and that nobody changed it since?" That is provenance, and it is a much easier problem to engineer. Watermark vs provenance Watermark / detector Signed provenance Where it lives hidden inside the content a small record next to the content What it claims "this probably came from model X" "this exact file came from source Y at time T" Survives edits?
articles.author: IndiaInfraNotes

articles.title: How Business Call Routing Systems Work: A Beginner's Guide
articles.excerpt: When you build or launch a small product, early user and client communications are dead simple: your phone rings, you pick it up, answer a question, and solve a problem. Why Call Routing Matters Concu…
articles.body: When you build or launch a small product, early user and client communications are dead simple: your phone rings, you pick it up, answer a question, and solve a problem. As transaction volumes climb and your customer base scales, that ad-hoc setup breaks down fast. A single smartphone or direct phone line quickly becomes a major single point of failure (SPOF). To handle scale without drowning in support overhead, teams implement call routing systems. Call routing at its simplest is the programmatic process of directing an inbound voice call to a designated endpoint based on a set of predefined evaluation rules.

articles.title: Touch Grass Birder: a bird call identifier that works with no signal
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass. Touch Grass Birder is a bird call identifier that runs entirely on your own machine. You tap Listen, hold your…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass . What I Built Touch Grass Birder is a bird call identifier that runs entirely on your own machine. You tap Listen , hold your phone up for six seconds while a bird sings, and it tells you what you are hearing. Then you put the phone away and go look for the bird. That is the whole point: the screen is the shortest part of the experience. It is built for the places where phone apps usually give up. A trailhead with one bar. A tent before sunrise. A county park where the migrant warblers are passing through and you have no idea what you are listening to. What it does: Records six seconds of audio in the browser and encodes it to WAV on-device.

articles.title: How eBPF Actually Runs Inside the Linux Kernel: The Verifier, JIT, and BPF Maps
articles.excerpt: How eBPF Actually Runs Inside the Linux Kernel: The Verifier, JIT, and BPF Maps If you ask most developers how eBPF works, you usually get one of two answers: "It is a tiny virtual machine inside Linu…
articles.body: How eBPF Actually Runs Inside the Linux Kernel: The Verifier, JIT, and BPF Maps If you ask most developers how eBPF works, you usually get one of two answers: "It is a tiny virtual machine inside Linux, like a JVM for the kernel." "It is a way to run custom C code in the kernel without writing a kernel module." Both explanations miss the fundamental architecture. eBPF does not run inside an interpreter loop at runtime, and it definitely does not allow arbitrary C execution. If you could execute arbitrary C in kernel space, a single null pointer dereference or off-by-one loop would panic your entire operating system.

articles.body: In 1964, Italian director Sergio Leone redefined the Western with A Fistful of Dollars . Eschewing the relatively simplistic morality tales of earlier Westerns, Leone’s central gunslinger wasn’t a noble hero, but an opportunistic cad who uses two rival factions in an Old West town against each other in order to score a big payday. Despite the moral complexity of it all — or, more likely, because of it — the film became an international success and proved that audiences were ready for a new kind of Western, that Americans no longer had a monopoly on the genre, and that Clint Eastwood was a bankable star outside of television.

articles.title: ChatGPT users, your AI-written text will soon carry a hidden watermark
articles.excerpt: The days of using ChatGPT to write your assignments and reports may be coming to an end.
articles.body: Credit: Edgar Cervantes / Android Authority TL;DR ChatGPT-generated text will soon carry an invisible watermark, starting in Europe. OpenAI’s detector can identify the watermark, but edits and shorter text can make detection harder. If you use ChatGPT to write, your AI-generated text could soon be identifiable as such. For years, AI tools have made it easy to generate everything from images and audio to human-like text. While AI-generated images, videos, and audio can often be identified using dedicated detection tools, AI-written text has largely escaped the same level of scrutiny. ChatGPT, in particular, has become one of the most widely used tools for generating text that can closely mimic human writing.
